hook.text: These are ten thousand coffee shop wait times... and they're lopsided.

shape.text: Most people wait a few minutes. But about one in twenty waits half an hour or more.

center.text: The average wait is ten minutes, and the spread is about ten minutes too.

sample.text: Now pick thirty people at random, and average their waits.

drop.text: That one average becomes one block in a new chart.

repeat.text: Pick thirty more... and thirty more. After two thousand samples,

bell.text: the averages have piled up into a bell, centered on ten.

clt.text: That's the Central Limit Theorem. The waits stay lopsided. Only their AVERAGES turn normal.

any-shape.text: And it isn't about wait times. Die rolls are flat, and this population has two humps.

any-bell.text: Average thirty from either one... and the same bell appears.

thumb.text: You'll hear that thirty is always enough. That's a rule of thumb, not a law.

heavy.text: A heavy tail, like incomes, is still lopsided at thirty. It can take HUNDREDS before the bell shows.

spread.text: So what does sample size control? The spread. They all center on ten, but bigger samples pile up tighter.

numbers.text: Samples of five spread about four and a half minutes. Thirty, under two. And a hundred, about one.

rule.text: The spread is the population's spread over the square root of n. Four times the data halves it.

next.text: That spread is the standard error. And it's not the standard deviation.
